tip: With ने (ne), the verb agrees with what was written, not the writer: रामचरितमानस (Ramcharitmanas) is treated as feminine, so लिखी (likhi) – even though Tulsidas is a man.
Hindi runs two word stocks side by side: ज़िंदगी (zindagi) is the Persian-side word, जीवन (jeevan) the Sanskrit-side one. Same meaning – zindagi sounds everyday, jeevan formal or literary.
तक (tak) covers both 'by' and 'until'. शुक्रवार तक (shukravaar tak) is a deadline here – by Friday – but with an ongoing action the same तक reads as until. Context decides.
English makes a decision; Hindi takes one: फ़ैसला लिया (faisla liya = took a decision), with लेना (lena = to take) as the partner verb.
Hindi pairs its relatives: जिसने (jisne = whoever) must be answered by उसने (usne) in the second half. English drops the second pronoun – Hindi keeps both.
No 'would have' word here – the -ती (-ti) ending alone marks the unreal past: न होती... बर्बाद हो जाती (na hoti... barbaad ho jaati) = hadn't rained... would have been ruined.
